Case 40 · Competitive Strategy & Moats · Switching costs and lock-in

Farmaan Batch Systems: The Validated Cage

A teaching case. All named companies are fictional; real firms are market context only.

1. Sunday night, Nashik

At ten past eleven on Sunday, 8 November 2026, Tanmayee Panigrahi had the Satpur MIDC office to herself and three documents open. A letter from Indravati Formulations Ltd, dated 21 August: it would move its two Sikkim plants to a rival platform at the 1 December renewal and re-tender all seven in 2028. A dossier from Farmaan's own validation practice: moving one plant off the Farmaan Plant Record Suite would cost Indravati ₹172 lakh. And a third, from a Mumbai consultancy Indravati had hired, putting it at ₹55 lakh.

At half past nine on Monday, Tanmayee, Vice-President of Product, had to tell the operating review what Farmaan should do. Three dates would not move: Indravati's decision on 1 December; the Falaq Growth Partners term sheet, expiring 15 December; and 31 March 2028, when Farmaan's sole Indian rights to Ikai Instrumentation's driver middleware lapsed.

What unsettled her was not that Indravati might leave. For eleven years Farmaan had told investors, and itself, that a validated pharmaceutical system is almost impossible to displace; she had helped write the sentence. That afternoon she had read what moving Farmaan's own base onto a modern architecture would cost: more than the company's annual revenue.

2. Company history, and the decision of June 2019

Farmaan Batch Systems was founded in Nashik in March 2013 by Debjani Chakrabarti, a chemical engineer with nine years in quality assurance at a Dahej plant. The paper batch manufacturing record — a binder of weighings, signatures and deviations travelling from granulation to packing — was where inspections by the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the US Food and Drug Administration went wrong. Farmaan built an electronic batch record honouring 21 CFR Part 11 audit trails, with a laboratory system and a deviation workflow beside it.

By 2026 the Suite ran 183 plants for 109 customers. Formulators in the class of Sun Pharma, Cipla and Dr Reddy's Laboratories built in-house; Farmaan sold to the tier below, WHO-GMP exporters for whom a data-integrity observation was existential and a ₹62 lakh licence cheap insurance.

The decision that shaped everything came in June 2019. Farmaan had a working multi-tenant cloud prototype, and its customers' quality heads would not sign off on batch records leaving the plant. So Farmaan chose single-tenant on-premise: a validated build on each plant's own servers, qualified through installation, operational and performance qualification, then frozen under change control until the customer paid for the next one.

That built the moat, and the cage. Every installation became a regulated asset with its own validation file, re-certified users and qualified interfaces; and Farmaan could not ship a feature to 183 plants, only a release each of the 183 would have to revalidate at its own cost. Two later choices tightened it: the April 2021 Ikai exclusive, which made the interface library unmatched and rented; and, to win Indravati against Ingit Process Automation in August 2021, escalation capped at 5 per cent a year plus delivery of the complete machine-readable archive within 90 days of a written request, free. That last clause was called harmless at the time.

3. The industry

The market had four kinds of seller. Ingit Process Automation Ltd of Vadodara was the incumbent: a thirty-year-old automation house with India's largest validated installed base, slow releases, and a services arm that made leaving it expensive and joining it slow. Farmaan was the specialist that had taken share from Ingit since 2016. Ikshana Quality Cloud, founded in Ahmedabad in February 2024 by two ex-Freshworks engineers and a former qualified person from a Gujarat API plant, was the insurgent: multi-tenant validated cloud, a licence near half Farmaan's, a template promising go-live in eleven weeks, and an operator interface users of both called embarrassingly better.

The fourth kind arrived in January 2026. Feldmann Prozesssysteme GmbH of Mannheim opened an India-hosted validated instance and an Ahmedabad office, pitching one platform validated for CDSCO, EU Annex 11 and US FDA expectations together, serialisation through its Dutch partner Ingelhoven Serialisatie BV, and a changeover allowance of up to ₹45 lakh a plant in free validation services. A competitor offering to pay the switching cost was a new kind of competitor.

Regulation made the product necessary and the lock-in real. Batch records had to stay retrievable for shelf life plus one year — up to six years — so nobody could simply switch an old system off. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, raised questions about the operator biometric signatures Farmaan held on-premise, and GST shaped how the Gulf contracts were papered. Foreign exposure was small but loud: six export accounts, nine plants, ₹690 lakh of recurring revenue, of which ₹310 lakh of the ₹690 lakh export book, or 44.9 per cent, came from Ibtikar Pharma Industries LLC in Dubai.

4. The situation in detail

February 2025. Farmaan launched Anumati, a module for electronic approvals and regulatory-submission export. Its purpose, in Tanmayee's memo: make Farmaan the system filings are generated from, so that leaving would mean rebuilding a submission pipeline. Belief: most of the base within eighteen months. Twenty-one months on, Anumati had produced at least one submission at 12 of the 183 plants — 6.6 per cent (Exhibit 5). The blocker was revalidation, competing for the hours inspections needed.

October 2025. Firoza Drugs & Intermediates Ltd of Baddi, a three-plant API maker and eight-year customer, moved a plant to Ikshana. Barnali Praharaj's team logged a contained loss and kept Firoza in the retained-logo count. Belief: the defection would fail on validation. In June 2026 the Ikshana plant cleared a CDSCO inspection with no data-integrity observations, and Firoza's quality head said so at an Ahmedabad forum, Indravati's people present.

August 2026. Indravati's letter arrived. Farmaan's largest account: seven plants — two at Ahmedabad, two in Sikkim, one each at Dahej, Baddi and Pithampur — 340 validated interfaces, about 1,900 users. It paid ₹640 lakh a year, which is 9.1 per cent of Farmaan's ₹7,000 lakh of recurring revenue. Ikshana had bid ₹38 lakh a plant, all-in, against the ₹79.5 lakh a plant Indravati effectively paid in Sikkim.

September 2026. Ipsita Samal's practice produced the dossier, and on Tanmayee's advice Farmaan gave it to Indravati's quality function, not procurement. Belief: the number would end the conversation. Instead Indravati had Fehrist Compliance Advisors mark it, Fehrist returned ₹55 lakh a plant, and Indravati's CFO had circulated that figure ever since.

October 2026. Subhendu Rath costed the cloud rebuild: ₹34 crore of engineering over 27 months, plus ₹40.26 crore — 183 plants at ₹22 lakh each — to revalidate the base onto it: ₹74.26 crore against ₹70 crore of recurring revenue and ₹21 crore of cash. That week Aritra Ghosh, modelling churn in Toronto, found the likeliest churn was not Indravati but the 64 single-plant Tier C accounts, 71 plants between them, at an average ₹18.0 lakh a plant, where validation files were thin and switching costs close to nothing.

5. The people

Tanmayee Panigrahi — VP Product, Nashik. The moat is a story the company stopped testing. Owns Anumati adoption (Exhibit 5). Not saying: she is why the dossier went to Indravati's quality team, and so why Fehrist was ever engaged.
Debjani Chakrabarti — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Nashik. Hold price: a discount to the largest account becomes the ceiling for the other 108. Not saying: Falaq wants an IPO track, and a company that cannot upgrade its own base lists badly.
Subhendu Rath — VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Nothing matters until the architecture changes; the ₹34 crore rebuild is his plan. Not saying: his ₹22 lakh a plant figure comes from four migrations, three at plants with fewer than 30 interfaces.
Ipsita Samal — Head of Validation and Regulatory Services, Ahmedabad. The ₹172 lakh is conservative, Fehrist's ₹55 lakh negligent. Her practice bills ₹8 crore a year, of which ₹3.4 crore of the ₹8 crore services line, 42.5 per cent, comes from migrating customers off competitors. Not saying: it also bills any revalidation an Anumati rollout triggers, so both outcomes suit her.
Barnali Praharaj — Customer Success Lead, Asia-Pacific, Singapore. Savable at a 27 per cent concession for a four-year lock. Her variable pay rides on logo retention, the left column of Exhibit 6. Not saying: under her definitions Firoza counts as retained.

7. Voices

"Price is not the point. If your own services people tell my auditors a changeover costs one seventy-two a plant, and a firm my CFO trusts tells him fifty-five, one of you is managing my risk and the other my budget, and I must choose which goes in the board pack."

Prabir Jena, Indravati Formulations, video call, 14 October 2026

"Match it on the two Sikkim lines. Losing the logo costs more than eighty-three lakh a year."

"Dean, if we match at Sikkim in November, Tier B knows by January. Sixty-two plants renew before September."

"Do not call our interface library a barrier in a customer deck again. We rent it. Ikai can license the same drivers to Ikshana from April 2028, and I am told they have discussed it."

"In Sikkim I watched three operators write weighings on paper and key them in at the end of the shift. That is the thing we call lock-in. It is not loyalty. It is a queue of people waiting for someone to make it stop."

Henrike Sallandt, Berlin, trip report, 21 September 2026

8. The options as Tanmayee currently sees them

  1. Hold price and litigate the number. Publish a defensible ₹172 lakh with its basis stated and take it to Indravati's chief executive over Prabir Jena's head. Protects the price ceiling for the other 108 accounts. Rests on a figure from the practice that profits from migrations — and on arguing in writing that Farmaan's archive is hard to leave, weeks before asking Falaq to fund a platform whose promise is easy upgrades.
  2. Concede ₹43 lakh on the Sikkim pair for a four-year lock across all seven plants, Anumati rollout written in as an obligation. Takes the three-year Sikkim cost to ₹348 lakh and buys what Farmaan has never had: a commitment to deploy the module that would make the next renewal harder to lose. Sets the reference price the moment it leaks, and commits Ipsita's practice to seven unscheduled revalidations.
  3. Let the two Sikkim plants go and sell the archive. Offer a read-only retention licence at ₹18 lakh a plant to satisfy the six-year record rule, keeping ₹36 lakh of the ₹159 lakh with no delivery obligation. Turns a regulatory requirement into recurring revenue — and teaches Indravati, cheaply thanks to the 2021 export clause, how much of the difficulty was real.
  4. Refuse to treat this as an account decision. Take the ₹34 crore rebuild to the board as the only item. Requires approving ₹74.26 crore against ₹70 crore of recurring revenue and ₹21 crore of cash, on an estimate extrapolated from four projects, while the interface exclusivity runs down.

She had written the four out twice, and both times the list itself bothered her. Every option answered how to keep Indravati, or how to stop asking. None addressed Aritra's finding that the churn risk sat in Tier C, where 71 plants and ₹1,280 lakh were held by nothing much at all. None said what Farmaan would sell in April 2028. And all four took the cost of leaving as a quantity to be estimated, when the two estimates differed by a factor of three and both came from parties paid for the answer.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Indravati's decision was due 1 December, and clause 9.2 obliged Farmaan to hand over the complete machine-readable archive within 90 days of a written request, free, whatever Monday decided. The Falaq term sheet — ₹180 crore for 13.5 per cent of a ₹1,330 crore post-money valuation — expired 15 December. FY26 closed with revenue of ₹78 crore, being ₹70 crore of recurring licence and ₹8 crore of validation services, and EBITDA of ₹6.2 crore, a margin of 7.9 per cent. Cash stood at ₹21 crore.

Farmaan employed 412 people: 168 in engineering, 96 in the validation practice, 54 in customer success, 61 in sales and marketing, 33 in administration. Sixty-two Tier B plants renewed before September 2027. Ibtikar's three Dubai plants renewed on 31 March 2027 and wanted Gulf dossier templates Farmaan did not have. And every release had to clear change control before it ran a batch, so nothing decided on Monday would reach an operator in Sikkim before the second quarter of FY28.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 2 and 4, what does Indravati gain and give up by moving the two Sikkim plants to Ikshana, and which switching-cost estimate would you rely on?
  2. Exhibit 6 reports two retention rates and two net revenue retention figures for one year. Which basis better describes the durability of Farmaan's relationships, and what does the choice of unit conceal?
  3. Exhibit 5 was meant to show Farmaan deepening its hold on customers. Read as a rate chain, what does it show, and where would you intervene?
  4. The 2019 decision raised the cost of leaving Farmaan and the cost of Farmaan changing anything. When is that trade a good one, and has Farmaan passed the point where it is not?
  5. Feldmann offers ₹45 lakh a plant to absorb a changeover, and the Ikai exclusivity lapses in April 2028. What, if anything, still keeps an Indravati plant on the Suite in 2029?
  6. It is Monday morning. What should Tanmayee recommend, and in what order should the renewal, the concession precedent, the rebuild and the term sheet be decided? What would she tell the board about how much of Farmaan's retention was a moat, and how much a market not yet offered an alternative?

The rest of Sunday night

At twenty past midnight Tanmayee did the arithmetic again on the back of the dossier: 159 a year, 76 a year, 83 of saving, 344 of friction on one estimate and 110 on the other, four years of payback or a little over one. Under it she wrote 34 crore, 40.26 crore, 21 crore of cash.

Prabir Jena had said twice in October that Farmaan's deviation workflow was the best in India, and that this was not why he was moving Sikkim. Aritra's model said the danger was 71 plants nobody would mention on Monday.

She closed the dossier, put the arithmetic in her bag and switched off the corridor light. She had nine hours, and did not know which option she would open with, or whether the list was the right list.

Case 20 · Competitive Strategy & Moats · Switching Costs and Lock-in

Vatsala Dairy Systems: The Vrindaban Renewal

Kolhapur, Maharashtra — 14 September 2026. Pranav Kothari, product manager at Vatsala Dairy Systems, read the letter from Vrindaban Sahakari Dugdh Sangh a second time before forwarding it to his VP. The district milk union — Vatsala's largest single account — wanted to know, in writing, why it should renew its software contract on 15 October at the existing price when a competitor had offered to run the same operations for 40 per cent less. The Sangh's board would vote on 6 October, three weeks away, in the middle of the flush season that carries the union's milk collection through Navratri into Diwali. Pranav had until then to give the union's managing director a business case the board could defend to its own members.

Company background

Vatsala Dairy Systems was founded in Kolhapur in 2015 by two engineers who had built reporting tools for a state dairy federation. Its product, the Vatsala Sahakari Suite, runs the back office of a milk cooperative: it reads fat and SNF readings from Automatic Milk Collection Units installed at village societies, computes each farmer's payment twice a month, pushes that payment as a direct transfer into the farmer's bank account, and produces the ledgers that state dairy development auditors and the cooperative's own elected board expect to see. By 2026 the Suite served 46 district-level unions across Maharashtra, Gujarat, Karnataka and Rajasthan, alongside larger federations such as Gujarat's Amul and Karnataka's Nandini, which run their own bespoke systems, and against dairy-technology firms such as Bengaluru's Stellapps. Vrindaban Sahakari Dugdh Sangh, an hour from Kolhapur, had been on the Suite for six years and was, by revenue, Vatsala's biggest customer.

The situation

The challenger was Vaikhari Farm Cloud, a Pune-based dairy-software startup founded in 2022 that had already taken three smaller unions in Rajasthan away from local vendors with a cheaper, cloud-native product and a farmer-facing mobile app with a noticeably better interface than Vatsala's. Vaikhari's written bid to Vrindaban proposed an annual fee of ₹108 lakh against Vatsala's current ₹180 lakh — a saving the board, facing elections in which a rival faction campaigned on "the union pays too much to a private software company," found useful to wave before its 94,000 farmer-members.

Balasaheb Patil, Vrindaban's managing director, was not eager to switch. He had told Pranav privately that he trusted the Suite's payment accuracy and did not want to gamble with farmer payments during flush season. But he needed a number, not a feeling, to bring to a board that would otherwise vote on price alone. Pranav's own team saw the account from different vantage points. Mei-Lin Foo, who led customer success for Asia from Singapore and tracked account health scores across time zones, had flagged Vrindaban amber two months earlier on price sensitivity alone. Omkar Ranade, the Pune engineering lead who had built the AMCU and bank-transfer integrations, warned that Vaikhari's own migration timeline — barely five weeks — was unrealistic given how deeply the transfer pipeline was wired into two nationalised banks and the district cooperative bank. Grant Whitfield, the sales head in New Jersey, had watched an almost identical price war play out on a US agricultural-software account he still managed, and argued Vatsala should simply match the number. Lukas Bergmann, the Berlin designer who had just reskinned the farmer app, thought the real answer was to give the union something Vaikhari could not yet build, not a lower invoice.

The people

Pranav Kothari — Product Manager, Vatsala Dairy Systems, Kolhapur. Owns the renewal recommendation; wants a defensible answer, not just a lower price, before 6 October.
Balasaheb Patil — Managing Director, Vrindaban Sahakari Dugdh Sangh. Wants to keep the Suite's payment reliability through flush season but needs numbers his elected board will accept.
Mei-Lin Foo — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants an account-level answer she can apply consistently across the other 45 unions when their renewals come due.
Omkar Ranade — Engineering Lead, Pune. Wants Vatsala to be honest about how long a real migration takes and what could go wrong during it.

A timeline of the decision

The options

  1. Match Vaikhari's price. Cut the annual contract to roughly ₹108–115 lakh to beat the bid outright. This keeps the account and the logo, and answers the board's price complaint directly. But at ₹108 lakh, revenue barely covers Vatsala's cost to serve the account, and 45 other unions renewing over the next two years will expect the same cut once word travels through Maharashtra's cooperative circles — a precedent that would erode margin across the whole customer base, not just this one contract.
  2. Offer a moderate concession bundled with a deeper integration, and share the true switching cost with the board. Propose the 15 per cent, three-year-lock price in Exhibit 3, and pair it with a new integration — linking farmer payments directly to a state dairy subsidy disbursal scheme that only Vatsala is currently certified to connect to — while giving Patil's board the migration-cost estimate in Exhibit 2 to weigh against Vaikhari's headline number. This preserves a defensible margin and raises the real cost of leaving in future cycles, but commits Omkar's team to building the new integration before Diwali, pulling engineering time from other roadmap work, and it may still lose to Vaikhari's cheaper bid if the board decides on politics rather than arithmetic.
  3. Let the account go. Decline to discount, redirect the account team's effort toward smaller, faster-growing unions, and treat the loss as pruning a large but low-margin, politically volatile customer. This frees capacity and avoids starting a price war Vatsala cannot win everywhere at once, but it surrenders 12.5 per cent of national ARR overnight, signals to the other 45 unions that Vatsala will not fight for a renewal, and hands 94,000 farmers' payment continuity, mid flush season, to a vendor that has never run a cutover this large.

Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 3, what exactly does Vrindaban gain and give up by switching to Vaikhari once the ₹90 lakh one-time switching cost is included?
  2. Which of the costs in Exhibit 2 would show up in a spreadsheet the board can see, and which real costs of switching — the ones Balasaheb Patil worries about privately — would not appear in any such table?
  3. If Vatsala matches Vaikhari's price outright, as in Option 1, what does that decision commit the company to when the other 45 district unions reach their own renewal dates?
  4. Given the people, the numbers, and the 6 October deadline, which of the three options should Pranav recommend to his VP, and why?

A note for the learner

Switching costs are one of the seven powers precisely because they let a firm keep a customer without having to be the cheapest option every year. But this case is built so that the tabulated switching cost is not, by itself, enough: Exhibit 2's ₹90 lakh looks large in isolation, yet spread over three years it amounts to about ₹30 lakh a year — far smaller than the ₹72 lakh annual gap between Vatsala's current price and Vaikhari's bid. A reader who stops at Exhibit 3's arithmetic will conclude that Vrindaban should switch, full stop. That is the trap of treating lock-in as something to measure once and rely on passively.

The stronger reading notices two things the spreadsheet cannot fully price: the switching costs that are real but not in Exhibit 2 — the risk of a payment error to 94,000 farmers during the flush season that carries the union through Diwali, and the loss of six years of audit trust with the state dairy department — and the fact that lock-in can be actively deepened, not just inherited. A defensible recommendation for Pranav is Option 2: offer the sustainable 15 per cent concession, and simultaneously build the state-subsidy integration that gives Vrindaban a reason to stay that Vaikhari cannot yet match, while being transparent with Patil's board about the migration risk rather than letting Vaikhari's headline number go unanswered. Option 1 protects this one account by starting a margin war Vatsala cannot afford across 46 unions; Option 3 abandons a defensible position without testing it. Option 2 is the one that treats switching costs as a power to be built, not merely observed.

Switching Costs and Lock-In

Strategy & Business › Competitive Strategy & Moats — the near-expert treatment: what lock-in is actually worth once you subtract what you paid for it and what a rival will pay to destroy it.

1. Two rooms, three weeks apart

On the morning of 11 August 2026, Kavya Raghunathan, chief product officer of Hiranya Diagnostics Systems, stood in front of a whiteboard in the company's Guindy office in Chennai with a single question written on it: what is our installed base actually worth? Hiranya had been selling benchtop clinical-chemistry and immunoassay analysers to Indian diagnostic chains and hospital laboratories since 2009. By FY26 it had 1,140 analysers in the field and revenue of ₹418 crore, of which ₹96 crore came from instruments at a gross margin of 22 percent, ₹278 crore from closed-system reagent packs at 61 percent, and ₹44 crore from service contracts and its cloud laboratory information system, Hiranya Vault, at 68 percent. The business was, in the textbook phrase, a razor-and-blade: the analyser was sold near cost so that the reagents could be sold at a margin the customer had no practical way to escape, because the instrument accepted only Hiranya's cartridges and only Hiranya's calibration protocol.

The question on the whiteboard was not academic. Hiranya's largest account — a 62-laboratory chain headquartered in Hyderabad, running 84 Hiranya analysers and spending ₹7.10 crore a year across reagents, service and Vault — had received a proposal from a challenger. The challenger sold open-system analysers that accepted third-party reagents from any CDSCO-registered supplier, quoted a cost per test roughly 34 percent below Hiranya's, and had offered to fund the migration in full: instrument placement at no capital cost, interface rebuilds by its own engineers, the termination liability on the Vault contract absorbed, and a dedicated team to re-run method comparisons. The chain's capital refresh cycle put its analyser replacement window at month 54 of the current fleet's life. Hiranya was at month 39. Kavya had fifteen months, a chief financial officer, Suresh Iyengar, who believed the account was safe because "they cannot physically leave," and a board paper due on 30 September asking whether Hiranya should launch an open-channel analyser line of its own — a proposal that would voluntarily dismantle the single largest switching cost the company possessed.

Three weeks later and 570 kilometres away, on 4 September 2026, Aparna Krishnan, head of product at Harshad Systems in Bengaluru, was having a version of the same argument with a very different shape. Harshad Systems, founded in 2023, sold Harshad Desk, an AI-native agentic support platform used by Indian insurers and direct-to-consumer brands to resolve claim-status, pre-authorisation and returns conversations without a human in the loop. Forty-one customers, ₹62 crore of annual recurring revenue, and one account that mattered more than the rest: a Mumbai-headquartered standalone health insurer paying ₹4.80 crore a year to run 2.9 lakh conversations a month across Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and English. The insurer's operations head, Farida Qureshi, had been approached by a rival whose pitch contained a claim Aparna found genuinely alarming. The rival did not promise a better model. It promised a migration agent: point it at Harshad's exported conversation logs and API schemas, and it would reconstruct the workflows, the routing rules and the response policies in eleven days. In 2023 that migration would have taken fourteen weeks of human work. Harshad's CEO, Nikhil Bose, wanted to respond by putting a three-year term with a 50 percent termination fee into every renewal. Aparna wanted to do the opposite: ship a complete, documented, one-click export of every conversation, policy and evaluation set the customer had ever created, and say so publicly.

Both executives believed they were reasoning about switching costs. Both were right that the concept was central. But the two situations sit at opposite ends of a distinction that the ordinary treatment of the topic obscures, and the argument of this page is that the distinction is the whole game. Lock-in is not worth what it costs a customer to leave. It is worth what it costs a customer to leave, minus the part a well-funded challenger can simply pay off, minus whatever you already surrendered at the front of the relationship to acquire the customer in the first place. That residue — and only that residue — is a moat. Everything else is either arithmetic a rival can undo with a cheque, or rent you have already given away without noticing.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

A switching cost is the one-time cost a customer bears in moving from an incumbent supplier to a substitute, over and above the price of the substitute itself. Lock-in is the strategic state that results when those costs are large enough, relative to the gains on offer, that a customer who would prefer the rival's product on the merits continues buying from the incumbent. Those definitions are uncontroversial. What is contested — and has been for nearly forty years — is whether lock-in produces durable excess returns for the supplier, and whether it is a form of value creation or of value extraction.

The formal literature begins with Paul Klemperer's 1987 paper in the Quarterly Journal of Economics and the body of work that followed it, including Joseph Farrell and Carl Shapiro's 1988 analysis of dynamic competition with switching costs, Alan Beggs and Klemperer's 1992 model of duopoly with an infinite horizon, and the 2007 survey Farrell and Klemperer wrote for the Handbook of Industrial Organization. The central result is not the one most practitioners quote. Klemperer's models show that a market with switching costs behaves like a sequence of separate auctions, one per customer, in which firms bid aggressively ex ante for the right to harvest ex post. He named the resulting price path "bargains-then-ripoffs." The uncomfortable corollary is that if the ex-ante competition is vigorous and buyers are forward-looking, the expected value of the ex-post rent gets competed away at the moment of acquisition. Lock-in still makes market shares sticky and prices higher on average, but it does not necessarily make anyone richer — it merely moves where the money is spent, from the renewal to the pitch.

Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian's Information Rules (1999) translated this for a technology audience and added two ideas practitioners use constantly without attribution. The first is that the value of an installed base is approximately the total switching costs of that base — the sum, across customers, of what it would cost each of them to leave plus what it would cost the supplier to replace them. The second is the lock-in cycle: brand selection, sampling, entrenchment, lock-in, and then a re-evaluation event that returns the customer to brand selection, at which point the cycle begins again. Hamilton Helmer's 7 Powers (2016) then placed switching costs among the seven structural sources of advantage — and, importantly, attached a caveat that is routinely dropped when the framework is taught. Helmer's own position is that switching costs confer Power only on existing customers, only on repeat purchases, and only where the incumbent can convert the barrier into either a price premium or a superior win rate on incremental sales. They do nothing to help a firm win new customers, and in a market where most future revenue is still unsold, a switching-cost moat protects a shrinking share of the prize.

Against that stands a marketing and customer-equity tradition — Frederick Reichheld's loyalty work, Blattberg and Deighton's customer-equity accounting, and the empirical typology of switching costs built by Burnham, Frels and Mahajan in 2003, which grouped them into procedural, financial and relational families and demonstrated that relational costs predicted retention better than financial ones in most consumer categories. This school signs the proposition that switching costs and satisfaction are complements: a satisfied customer with high switching costs is nearly unbreakable, while a dissatisfied customer with high switching costs is a liability waiting for a trigger. It refuses to sign the proposition that lock-in is a substitute for product quality.

A third position, broadly the Chicago-school and contestability view, holds that rational buyers price expected lock-in into the original purchase, so engineered switching costs are self-defeating in any market with informed buyers and repeated interaction. Its representatives would sign the claim that aftermarket power is generally competed away at the equipment sale; they would not sign it in the presence of information asymmetry or high measurement costs, which is precisely the exception the US Supreme Court carved out in Kodak v. Image Technical Services in 1992 when it allowed that a firm with no power in the equipment market could still hold power in the aftermarket for parts and service.

A fourth position is regulatory and has become the most consequential of the four in India. It treats engineered switching costs as a consumer-welfare problem and legislates them away. Mobile number portability arrived under TRAI in 2011 and removed a switching cost the telecom industry had relied on for a decade; IRDAI made health-insurance portability mandatory the same year; the Reserve Bank's Account Aggregator framework made financial data portable by design; NPCI's interoperable UPI and QR standards dissolved proprietary acceptance networks; and ONDC exists explicitly to make commerce catalogues portable across platforms. A practitioner who builds a business on a switching cost that a regulator can abolish with a circular is running a different risk from the one on the strategy slide. It is worth noting precisely, because it is often misstated, that India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 — unlike the 2019 draft that preceded it, and unlike Article 20 of the European GDPR — does not carry a general right to data portability. That is a live gap, not a settled position.

The schools do not disagree about what a switching cost is. They disagree about who ends up with the money.

3. Mechanics in depth: the arithmetic of what lock-in is worth

The competent practitioner's model of switching costs is a list of sources and a total. The expert's model has three additional moving parts: a filter for what a challenger can purchase, a subtraction for what was given away at acquisition, and a clock. Take them in order.

Start from the five sources that any working practitioner can name — contractual, technical, data, procedural, relational — and add a sixth that matters enormously in regulated categories and is usually missed: revalidation cost, the cost of re-establishing compliance after a change of system. The first analytical move is not to total them. It is to ask, source by source, can a challenger with a chequebook make this go away? Contractual termination fees can be bought down for exactly their face value; that is what they are. Integration rebuilds can be bought down at the challenger's engineering cost, which in 2026 is falling fast. Data migration can be bought down where schemas are standard and bought down only partly where they are not. Procedural retraining can be subsidised but not eliminated, because the customer's people still have to spend the hours. Revalidation under an accreditation regime often cannot be bought at any price, because what it consumes is calendar time and an assessor's availability, neither of which responds to money. Relational trust and the personal career exposure of the individual who signs the migration off cannot be bought at all.

Contractual lock-in sits at the wrong end of this spectrum — it is the source that is easiest to build, easiest for a rival to pay off, and most resented by the customer who pays it.

With that filter in place the arithmetic becomes tractable. Let S be the customer's perceived total switching cost, Sp the portion a challenger can purchase away, and B the challenger's affordable buy-down budget — which is bounded above by the present value of the gross margin the challenger expects to earn on the account, since no rational competitor spends more to win an account than the account is worth. The effective barrier is then:

E = S − min(B, Sp)
and the maximum annual price premium the incumbent can sustain over a horizon of n years at discount rate r is
p ≤ E ⁄ a(n, r), where a is the ordinary annuity factor.
Finally, the rent actually earned is R = PV(p over n) − D, where D is the acquisition subsidy: the discounts, free implementation and forgone margin spent to win the customer.

Two things follow immediately, and they are the two things practitioners miss. First, E depends on the challenger's economics, not only on yours. A barrier of ₹1 crore is a fortress against a rival whose lifetime gross margin on the account is ₹40 lakh and a speed bump against a rival whose lifetime gross margin is ₹9 crore. Any statement of the form "our switching costs are high" that does not name a challenger and its budget is not an analysis. Second, if D is large — and in competitive enterprise sales it usually is — the rent can be zero or negative even when the barrier is genuinely formidable. This is Klemperer's rent-dissipation result arriving on a real invoice.

The reagent margin was real, but it was not a moat premium; it was the repayment schedule on a loan Hiranya had made to its own customer five years earlier, and it had not yet cleared.

This is the second-order effect that deserves a name, because it explains more strategic behaviour than any other consequence of lock-in: the harvest reflex. Klemperer's models predict that a firm with a large locked-in base rationally raises prices and under-invests in winning new customers, while a firm with a small base rationally invests in acquisition. Each firm is optimising correctly; the aggregate outcome is that incumbents cede the growing, unlocked segment of the market to entrants and then discover, five years later, that the segment they ceded was the market. The organisational tell is visible in the compensation plan long before it is visible in the revenue: when the renewals desk is compensated on gross retention and the new-logo team is compensated on bookings, and the renewals desk is winning the internal argument about roadmap priority, the harvest reflex has already taken hold.

The third moving part is the clock. Every source of switching cost has a decay function, and the aggregate is not monotonic. Contractual costs decay linearly to zero as the term runs out. Procedural fluency decays with staff attrition: at the 19 percent annual attrition typical of Indian laboratory and back-office roles, only about half the originally trained cohort remains after three years, and the half that remains has trained the other half imperfectly. Technical costs decay as standards emerge — GSTN's e-invoice schema, HL7 and the ABDM health-data standards, the Account Aggregator specification each converted a proprietary integration into a commodity one. And in hardware, the curve does not decay at all: it climbs steadily and then falls off a cliff on a date that is known years in advance, because the customer's own depreciation schedule says so.

4. When the idea applies, and when it actively misleads

Five conditions, stated as claims that can be falsified with evidence a product organisation can actually gather. First: the customer's perceived switching cost exceeds the value gap multiplied by the remaining horizon. For Hiranya, the challenger's 34 percent cost-per-test advantage on ₹6.20 crore of reagents is roughly ₹2.11 crore a year — over even two years that dwarfs a ₹1.77 crore barrier, so the condition fails on any horizon longer than about ten months. For Harshad, the rival's pricing advantage is modest, maybe 12 percent, but the barrier is so small that the condition also fails. Both protagonists are, on this test, exposed.

Second: a material share of the barrier is not purchasable. Hiranya passes decisively — 54 percent of its barrier sits in revalidation and procedural lines that money cannot compress. Harshad fails badly: of a ₹1.05 crore estimated switching cost, ₹0.95 crore is workflow rebuild, integration and data reload, every rupee of which a migration agent can now absorb. Third: the rent has not already been dissipated at acquisition. Hiranya fails; Harshad, which sells on 12-month rolling terms with a light-touch implementation, actually passes, because it never bought the account with a subsidy. Fourth: there is no scheduled reset inside the decision horizon. Hiranya fails — the reset is fifteen months away and on the customer's calendar. Fifth: the customer's realistic alternative is leaving, not multi-homing. Here Harshad fails in the most modern way: Farida Qureshi's actual plan, she eventually admitted, was not to replace Harshad but to route pre-authorisation conversations to the rival while leaving claim-status on Harshad, and compare resolution rates for two quarters. There is no switching event to defend against at all.

The conditions under which the whole frame becomes actively misleading are worth stating plainly, because a competent practitioner will reach for switching-cost reasoning in all of them. In a category growing faster than about 40 percent a year, most future revenue is unsold, and a moat that protects only the installed base is a moat around a small and shrinking field. Where a regulator has declared portability a right — telecom, health insurance, retail payments, financial data in India already — a switching cost is a liability with a countdown on it. Where the buying decision is made by an agent on behalf of a principal, the dominant switching cost is the agent's personal exposure, which is not in any of the five categories and does not respond to product improvements. And where purchase frequency is low — capital equipment, enterprise suites replaced every seven years — entrenchment never gets deep enough to matter within the sales cycle, and the concept simply has nothing to say.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the organisational seams

Multi-product bundles. Selling a suite raises the switching cost superadditively, because leaving requires replacing every module at once. It also converts what were n independent, small, uncorrelated churn events into one large correlated one. Expected retention improves; the variance of revenue loss gets much worse. Hiranya learned this in a smaller way when a defect in Vault's HL7 connector in early 2026 caused a mid-sized Kochi customer to reopen not just the LIS contract but the reagent contract with it. The expert's formulation: a bundle is a leveraged position on your own worst module.

Two-sided and marketplace businesses. Practitioners chronically confuse cross-side network effects with switching costs here. The reason a seller stays on a marketplace because the buyers are there is a network effect — a forward-looking, shared value that a rival with equal liquidity would match. The reason the same seller stays because four years of ratings, review history and search-ranking signal are not portable is a switching cost — private, backward-looking, and specific to that seller's own accumulated record. The distinction has operational teeth: network effects are defeated by a rival who gets liquidity, switching costs by a rival who gets portability. ONDC's entire design premise is that the second of these can be legislated even where the first cannot.

Regulated categories. The regulator can create switching costs as easily as it can destroy them. NABL's requirement that a laboratory revalidate its measurement scope after a change of analytical method is not something Hiranya invented, and it is worth roughly ₹86 lakh of barrier on the Hyderabad account. Building a strategy on a regulator-created barrier is more durable than building one on a contract clause and less durable than it feels, because the same regulator can standardise the validation pathway in a single revision.

Hardware plus software. The defining property is that the barrier is lumpy and scheduled rather than continuous. The customer's finance team knows to the quarter when the asset comes off the books, and that date is when the entire accumulated barrier resets to near zero. The correct managerial response is counterintuitive: the incumbent should spend most aggressively on deepening non-hardware lock-in — data, workflow, peer benchmarking — in the eighteen months before the reset, precisely when the harvest reflex is telling it to raise prices instead.

AI-native products. Here the field has not settled, and the honest summary is that artificial intelligence is simultaneously the most promising new source of switching cost and the most powerful solvent of old ones. On the solvent side: schema mapping, integration rewriting, prompt reconstruction and documentation regeneration are exactly the tasks at which coding agents have become competent, which means the technical and data lines of every incumbent's barrier are being repriced downward each quarter. Aparna's rival was not bluffing about eleven days. On the source side: what remains non-purchasable in an AI product is accumulated preference data — the record of which resolutions a particular insurer's compliance team accepted and rejected, the evaluation sets built from its own edge cases, the calibration of when the agent should escalate to a human. That is a genuine asset. But it carries a failure mode with no analogue in traditional software: leapfrog risk. A barrier built on a fine-tuned model can evaporate entirely when a frontier model arrives that is better out of the box than the incumbent's tuned system, at which point eighteen months of accumulated tuning becomes a liability rather than an asset.

The organisational seams. Ask who owns switching costs in any company of more than 200 people and the answer is nobody. Legal owns the termination clause. Sales owns the term length. Finance owns the discount. Product owns the integrations. Customer success owns the relationship and reports on satisfaction. The only one of these with a named owner, a number and a quarterly review is the contractual line — which is why, in company after company, the contractual line is the only one that gets deliberately managed, and it is the weakest and most resented of the five. Mature companies do not solve this with a framework; they solve it by moving two specific numbers into a single owner's scorecard — the per-account accrual rate of non-purchasable barrier, and the competitive win rate on new logos — and accepting that the two will trade off against each other.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The barrier is relative to a named challenger, never absolute

The competent practitioner produces a switching-cost estimate in rupees. The expert refuses to accept the number without a denominator: relative to whose budget? A ₹1.77 crore barrier on an account worth ₹1.80 crore of lifetime margin to a challenger is a wall; the same barrier on an account a strategic entrant is willing to lose ₹5 crore on to establish a reference customer in Indian diagnostics is a formality. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a retention slide that quotes switching cost as a single company-wide figure with no competitor named on it. The obvious reading — that a big number is a strong position — is wrong because it treats the customer's cost as a physical property of the relationship rather than as one side of a negotiation whose other side has a wallet.

You may already have sold the lock-in you think you own

Every rupee of front-loaded discount, free implementation, waived onboarding and absorbed migration is a prepayment against future lock-in rent, and in competitive markets the prepayment tends toward the full expected value of the rent. Hiranya's negative ₹33 lakh is not a pathology; Klemperer's models say it is the equilibrium. The tell is a business that reports strong gross retention and healthy renewal margins while its blended payback period quietly lengthens year after year. The obvious reading — that retention economics are excellent — is wrong because the margin being celebrated at renewal is repayment of capital, not return on it, and the accounting never separates the two.

Lock-in binds the vendor as tightly as the customer

The deeper a customer's workflow is entangled with your product, the less freedom you have to change that product. Every integration you build is an interface you must support forever; every behaviour a customer has automated against, including your bugs, becomes a specification you cannot revise. Hiranya could not change Vault's QC export format in 2025 because two hospital chains had built internal dashboards against it. The tell is a deprecation that has been on the roadmap for three consecutive planning cycles and keeps being deferred "because of one account." The obvious reading — that this is a prioritisation failure — is wrong; it is the cost of the moat being collected, on schedule, from the wrong side.

Manage the accrual rate, not the level

Switching cost is a stock, and stocks are not manageable; flows are. The expert's instrument is a per-account quarterly accrual: integrations added, records created, users trained to fluency, evaluation sets authored, reports that other people now depend on. A competent team reports "our average switching cost is ₹40 lakh." An expert team reports "we accrue ₹3.1 lakh of non-purchasable barrier per account per quarter for the first eight quarters, then ₹0.6 lakh thereafter" — and knows immediately that its onboarding, not its renewal motion, is where the moat is actually built. The tell is a retention dashboard with levels and no rates.

Perceived cost, not calculated cost, and the perceiver is a person with a career

The number that decides the outcome lives in the head of one individual, and that individual is usually not the economic buyer. For the Hyderabad chain it was Dr. Meera Sathe, the clinical head, whose exposure if a method change shifted reference ranges mid-year was personal, professional and uninsurable. That exposure did not appear on any ledger and was almost certainly the largest single number in the decision. The tell is a customer who declines a clearly superior economic offer without ever disputing the arithmetic — "not this year" delivered without a counter-number.

Customers minimise risk, not expected cost

The ledger model implicitly assumes expected-value maximisation. Real buyers are loss-averse and evaluate the tail. A 6 percent chance of a three-week claims outage during peak season is worth more to Farida Qureshi than the certain ₹58 lakh she would save, because the outage is career-ending and the saving is a line item. This is why incumbents who defend on price lose to incumbents who defend on demonstrated reliability under stress. The tell is customers using the vocabulary of risk — "we cannot afford for this to go wrong" — where your team hears the vocabulary of price.

Low churn is a lagging indicator; new-logo win rate is the leading one

A base held by switching costs will show excellent retention for years after the product has stopped being the right choice for a new buyer. The diagnostic that fires early is the cold-start test: your win rate in genuinely competitive new-logo evaluations, where no switching cost protects you. Hiranya's competitive win rate had fallen from 48 percent in FY23 to 29 percent in FY26 while gross retention stayed above 93 percent. The first number was telling the truth about the second, roughly three years ahead. The tell is a board pack where retention and win rate appear on different pages with different owners.

The question is share of workflow, not stay or leave

Multi-homing has made the binary obsolete in most software categories. The expert asks what fraction of the relevant workflow runs through the product, and watches the derivative. A customer whose seat count is flat while its category spend grows 30 percent has already switched — it has simply done so at the margin, invisibly, without a churn event. The tell is stable revenue with declining usage per rupee. The obvious reading — that the account is stable — is wrong because the account has been quietly reclassified from system of record to one of several tools.

Lock-in is a distribution, and the average is never the right number

Any base of more than fifty accounts contains hostages (high barrier, low satisfaction — the most dangerous segment a company can own), natives (high barrier, high satisfaction), tourists (low barrier, low commitment) and advocates (low barrier, high satisfaction, the segment that proves the product is genuinely good). These four require opposite actions, and the company average recommends a strategy correct for none of them. The tell is an across-the-board retention programme — a uniform discount, a uniform loyalty tier — deployed against a threat that is concentrated in one quadrant.

Keep a calendar of expiry dates

Contracts end, fleets are refreshed, trained staff resign, standards are published, CFOs are replaced, and each of these resets some part of the barrier on a date that is knowable in advance. The expert maintains, for the top twenty accounts, an explicit list of when each source next resets and what the barrier will be on the day after. The tell is simple and damning: ask when the company's moat next resets on its largest account, and watch whether anyone in the room can name a date.

7. How it varies by product type and company stage

Much of what is written about switching costs by product type is padding, because the arithmetic does not change: the formula E = S − min(B, Sp) holds identically in consumer, enterprise, marketplace, hardware and AI businesses. What changes is the composition of S, the identity and budget of the challenger, and the shape of the clock. That is genuinely all, and saying it plainly saves a great deal of confusion.

An early-scale company between ₹20 and ₹100 crore of revenue is at the point of maximum leverage, because its onboarding design determines the accrual rate of non-purchasable barrier for every cohort that follows, and nobody has yet institutionalised a bad answer. A scaled incumbent has the opposite problem: barriers are accumulating automatically, the harvest reflex is beginning to shape the roadmap, and the binding constraint is discipline about the new-logo win rate rather than about retention. Hiranya at ₹418 crore is squarely in the third category, and Harshad at ₹62 crore in the second — which is why Aparna's instinct to ship portability is defensible in a way it would not be at Hiranya, and why Nikhil Bose's instinct to add a three-year lock is exactly the institutionalised bad answer.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

The barrier that could not be bought: Hiranya's peer-comparison network. Hiranya Vault aggregates daily internal quality-control results from all 1,140 installed analysers and returns, to each laboratory, a peer-group median and standard deviation for every analyte on its menu — the comparison NABL assessors increasingly expect a laboratory to produce. A single lab leaving Hiranya loses access to peer medians drawn from roughly 3,100 instrument-analyte combinations and must substitute six months of internal-only data, which no assessor regards as equivalent. The challenger, with 40 installed analysers in India, cannot replicate this at any price inside three years, because the asset is not code or data-in-storage but a population. Priced at the ₹0.86 crore revalidation line in Table 1, this single feature accounts for 47 percent of Hiranya's residual barrier on the Hyderabad account — and it was built in 2019 as a customer-support convenience, not as a strategy.

The barrier that dissolved in eleven days: Harshad's second-largest account. In June 2026 Harshad lost a ₹1.90 crore D2C account to the same rival. The post-mortem was uncomfortably clean. Total switching cost estimated at ₹41 lakh: ₹14 lakh of workflow and prompt rebuild, ₹16 lakh of integration work against the customer's order-management and returns systems, ₹7 lakh of conversation-history reload, ₹4 lakh of supervisor retraining. Of that, ₹37 lakh was purchasable, and the rival's migration agent did most of it for an internal cost Harshad later estimated at under ₹6 lakh. The effective barrier was ₹4 lakh on a ₹1.90 crore account — two-tenths of one percent. The recovery, such as it was, taught Aparna the thing she took into the September argument: the only line item the agent could not touch was the ₹4 lakh of supervisor retraining and, buried in it, three months of calibration in which the customer's compliance lead had learned exactly when to trust the agent's judgement and when to override it. Trust calibration is the switching cost in an AI product. Everything else is a file transfer.

The failure, and what recovery actually cost: Himadri Retail Systems. Himadri sold point-of-sale and billing systems to multi-brand apparel retail from its Pune base, and by FY22 it ran 4,200 terminals across 380 chains, with revenue of ₹94 crore at 26 percent EBITDA. Its retention strategy was engineered lock-in in its purest form: five-year terms at ₹18,000 per terminal per year, a 55 percent termination fee on the unexpired portion, a proprietary receipt-printer and card-reader stack that worked only with Himadri software, and a ₹2.4 lakh "data extraction fee" for a full historical export. Between 2021 and 2023 three things happened at once. NPCI's interoperable UPI and QR standards made the proprietary card-reader stack worthless. GST e-invoicing standardised the transaction schema, so the data that had been expensive to export became trivially portable for everyone. And the 2018 cohort of five-year contracts — a third of the base, signed within nine months of each other — all expired inside the same four quarters. Gross retention fell from 94 percent in FY23 to 61 percent in FY24, and revenue to ₹57 crore.

The diagnosis is precise, not moral. Himadri's barrier was almost entirely purchasable and almost entirely on a schedule it had itself created by signing a cohort of identical terms in a single year — correlated expiry, the same error as a bank funding long assets with a single tranche of short liabilities. The recovery, under a new chief executive, Anand Vaidya, was slower and more expensive than any board expects. Himadri abolished the extraction fee, published a one-click export in the GSTN-compatible schema, cut the standard term to twelve months rolling, and — the part that mattered — rebuilt the product around a replenishment-forecasting layer that requires nine months of a store's own sales history before its recommendations beat a manager's judgement. That is an earned barrier: it is non-purchasable, because what it consumes is the customer's own elapsed time, and it accrues as a by-product of ordinary use. By FY26 gross retention had recovered to 88 percent and revenue to ₹71 crore, but EBITDA margin had fallen to 19 percent and the rebuild had taken 26 months and roughly ₹40 crore of cumulative operating profit. The moat came back. The valuation multiple did not.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

The failure modes below are not independent — the harvest reflex and the cold-start blindness usually travel together, and correlated expiry is what converts a slow problem into a sudden one — but each has a distinct early warning and a distinct diagnostic question, and it is worth being able to name them separately in a room.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether lock-in produces returns at all. The rent-dissipation position, in its strongest form, holds that in any market with competitive acquisition and reasonably forward-looking buyers, the expected value of future lock-in is bid into the acquisition price and earns the incumbent nothing beyond its cost of capital. Its evidence is Klemperer's formal results, the observed intensity of front-loaded discounting in enterprise software and telecom, and cases like Hiranya's where a careful reconstruction shows negative net rent. The Power position, in its strongest form, holds that this is true only where challengers can accurately forecast the barrier they are bidding for; where the barrier accrues unpredictably as a by-product of usage — nobody at Hiranya forecast the peer-comparison network in 2019 — the acquisition auction systematically underprices it, and the surplus accrues to the incumbent. For the dissipation view to be wrong, you need barriers that are large, durable and not foreseeable at the point of sale. That is a testable condition and it is satisfied more often than the theory predicts.

Whether engineered lock-in is ever legitimate. The easy position — earn it, never engineer it — is too easy. The strongest case for engineering runs: substantial up-front investment by a supplier (a twelve-week implementation, a hardware placement, a validation programme) is only financeable against a committed term, so a contract that binds the customer is what makes the investment possible at all, and the customer receives the benefit in a lower price. Symmetric commitment is not extraction. The opposing case observes that in practice the commitment is almost never symmetric: the customer's exit is penalised and the supplier's underperformance is not, and the moment that asymmetry exists the contract is transferring risk rather than financing investment. What would settle it is whether the supplier accepts a mirror-image service-credit obligation. Most do not, which tells you which case is usually being made.

Whether AI raises or lowers switching costs on net. One camp argues AI is the greatest solvent of lock-in in forty years, because the entire technical and data barrier is now automatable and the barrier will approach the cost of the compute. The other argues it is the greatest generator, because accumulated preference data, evaluation sets and human trust calibration are genuinely non-portable and compound faster than any previous asset. The evidence is thin and recent on both sides; Harshad's two accounts point in opposite directions within the same year. What is not in dispute is the direction of the variance: whichever camp is right, the dispersion between products with real accumulated preference assets and products with none is widening sharply.

Whether to make your exit excellent. The open-exit school argues that a documented, free, complete export wins deals at the moment of purchase — it removes the buyer's largest unspoken objection — costs nothing against a well-designed product, and forecloses the regulatory risk of being made to build it under duress. The friction school argues this is a fashionable way of unilaterally disarming, that no customer has ever chosen a vendor because of its export format, and that the deals supposedly won are unmeasurable while the accounts lost are not. Neither side has a clean natural experiment. Himadri's recovery is evidence for the first; it is also a single case, in a category where a regulator had already forced the issue.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied switching costs produces a five-source taxonomy, totals it, and concludes that the base is defensible. Someone who has internalised the idea does four things differently. They never state a barrier without naming the challenger it is a barrier against and estimating that challenger's budget, because they know the number is half of a negotiation and not a property of the product. They audit acquisition subsidy against realised premium before claiming any moat margin, because they have seen the arithmetic come out negative on a flagship account. They manage the accrual rate of non-purchasable barrier as an onboarding metric rather than the level as a retention metric, and they can name which product decision in the last two quarters raised or lowered it. And they keep the expiry calendar — contract terms, refresh dates, attrition-adjusted fluency, pending standards — because they treat the moat as an asset with a maturity schedule rather than as a permanent feature of the landscape.

There is a fifth, subtler behaviour. Experts are unusually relaxed about making exit easy and unusually anxious about the cold-start test. They will cheerfully ship a data export, and they will lose sleep over a new-logo win rate that has drifted down four points, because they have understood that a barrier buys time and nothing else. The only question that matters is what the company does with the time.

12. What each of them decided

Kavya Raghunathan's board paper on 30 September recommended launching the open-channel analyser line, over her chief financial officer's objection, on three grounds. The reagent barrier on the largest accounts was already fully purchasable and being purchased; the residual, non-purchasable barrier sat in revalidation and peer-comparison, neither of which required a closed reagent system to sustain; and Hiranya's competitive win rate of 29 percent said the closed system was costing more in lost new business than it was earning in protected reagent margin. She paired it with two commitments that mattered more than the headline: a standing programme to deepen the Vault peer-comparison network, extending it from quality control into turnaround-time and reference-interval benchmarking, and an instruction that the fifteen months before the Hyderabad chain's refresh would be spent adding non-purchasable value rather than harvesting price. Suresh Iyengar's dissent is recorded in the minutes and is not unreasonable: the open-channel line will cannibalise ₹60 to ₹90 crore of reagent revenue within three years against benefits that are, at the point of decision, projections.

Aparna Krishnan lost the argument about the three-year term and won the argument about portability, which she regarded as the correct trade. Harshad Desk now ships a complete export of conversations, policies and evaluation sets, and Harshad's sales team leads with it. What Aparna did with the concession was subtler: she moved three engineers onto a "calibration ledger" — a persistent, per-customer record of every override, escalation threshold and rejected resolution, surfaced back to the customer's own compliance team as an auditable artefact. It is exportable, in the sense that the file can be downloaded. It is not portable, in the sense that the rival's agent has nothing to do with it, because what it encodes is not data but a relationship between an insurer's risk appetite and a system's behaviour, accumulated one decision at a time. Whether that constitutes a moat or merely a delay is, on the evidence available in September 2026, genuinely unresolved.

  1. Hiranya's net lock-in rent on its largest account was negative ₹33 lakh, yet the account is profitable and the reagent margin is 61 percent. Is the negative figure the right basis for a strategic decision, or an accounting artefact of how the 2021 subsidy was allocated? What would change your answer?
  2. Aparna shipped portability and then built the calibration ledger. Is that a genuine non-purchasable barrier, or the same engineered friction in more sophisticated clothing — and what evidence, available within twelve months, would distinguish the two?
  3. Himadri's recovery restored retention but not margin. If you were on its board in 2024, would you have accepted 26 months and ₹40 crore of foregone profit to rebuild an earned barrier, or harvested the declining base and returned the capital?

13. Going deeper

  • Moats and the 7 Powers — places switching costs among the six other structural sources of advantage and, crucially, explains why most of them compound with each other; it unlocks the question of which combination a given business can realistically hold.
  • Multi-homing and competition — the direct successor to this page, because in most software categories the customer's answer to a barrier is no longer to leave but to add a second supplier, which makes share-of-workflow the operative metric.
  • Competitive analysis — supplies the missing denominator in every calculation here: the challenger's cost structure and lifetime margin, without which no barrier can be sized.
  • Right to win — asks whether you should be in the contest at all, which is the prior question to how well you can defend it, and prevents switching-cost reasoning from being used to justify a position that was never winnable.
  • Network effects — the idea most often confused with switching costs, and the confusion is expensive because the two are defeated by entirely different competitive moves.
  • Moats in the AI era — takes up the unresolved argument in section 10 about whether accumulated preference data is a durable asset or a fine-tune away from obsolescence.
  • Positioning — determines which alternative the customer measures you against, and therefore the size of the value gap that any barrier has to exceed.
  • Five forces and industry structure — locates switching costs in buyer power and entry barriers, and explains why regulators intervene in precisely the industries where they work best.

Switching Costs and Lock-In

Strategy & Business › Competitive Strategy & Moats — what keeps a customer from leaving once they have invested

A board that wants a price war

On the second Tuesday of September 2026, Rohan Mehta, vice-president of product at Shaurya Ledger Cloud, sat in a Pune conference room with a single slide on the screen behind him: a list of eleven customer accounts, three of them highlighted in red. Shaurya Ledger Cloud sold cloud accounting and GST-compliance software to small and mid-sized Indian manufacturers — the unglamorous plumbing of e-invoicing, GST return filing, and bank reconciliation that every registered business in the country has to get right every month or face notices from the tax department. The company had built a respectable base of 340 paying customers over four years, at an average contract of roughly ₹14 lakh a year, and it had just been told that a well-funded rival, Sumeru Books, was calling those eleven accounts directly with an offer: switch before the quarter closes, and Sumeru would cut the list price by 55 percent, waive the first three months entirely, and — this was the detail that had made Rohan sit up — handle the entire data migration and system integration at its own cost, with its own engineers, on its own timeline.

The account Rohan cared about most was Saroj Industries, a hosiery and knitwear manufacturer in Ludhiana with forty-two employees on the shop floor and six in accounts. Saroj had signed a two-year, ₹18-lakh-a-year contract with Shaurya fourteen months earlier, and its chief financial officer, a careful man named Devinder Anand, had called Rohan's account manager that morning to say, not unkindly, that he had a number from Sumeru in front of him and needed a reason not to act on it by Friday. The board's instinct, voiced twice in the meeting by the CEO, was to match the discount. Rohan's instinct was that matching the discount would be throwing away the one asset Shaurya actually had, and that the right response depended on a concept the company had never named out loud but had been quietly building for two years: switching costs, and the lock-in they produce. Getting the analysis wrong in either direction — discounting when discounting was not the issue, or assuming loyalty that was not really there — would cost Shaurya somewhere between ₹40 lakh and ₹1.5 crore in annual recurring revenue depending on how many of the eleven accounts walked.

The idea, stated precisely

A switching cost is the one-time cost — in money, time, risk, or forfeited value — that a customer incurs by moving from a supplier's product to a substitute, over and above whatever the substitute itself costs to buy. It is not what the incumbent charges the customer to leave; it is what leaving costs the customer regardless of what the incumbent charges. Lock-in is the resulting strategic condition: a state in which switching costs are high enough, relative to the gains on offer from an alternative, that a customer who might otherwise prefer a rival's product continues buying from the incumbent anyway. The idea was formalised by the Oxford economist Paul Klemperer in a 1987 paper on markets with consumer switching costs, which showed mathematically why such markets behave less like textbook competition — where price alone decides the winner — and more like a sequence of small, semi-captive auctions, one per customer, repeated at each renewal. Carl Shapiro and Hal Varian extended the idea for a technology audience in their 1999 book Information Rules, cataloguing the specific mechanisms — contracts, training, data, loyalty programmes, search costs — by which digital and information businesses generate lock-in deliberately. Hamilton Helmer's 2016 book 7 Powers later placed switching costs alongside scale economies, network effects, counter-positioning, branding, cornered resources, and process power as one of only seven durable sources of competitive advantage — the "moats" that keep a business's returns from being competed away. The sentence Rohan wanted to be able to say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: switching costs are the toll a customer pays to leave, and our job is to make sure that toll is paid for real value already delivered — not levied as a penalty invented at the exit door.

How it actually works

Switching costs do not arrive as a single number; they accumulate from several distinct sources, and a product leader who treats them as one undifferentiated blob will misdiagnose both the threat and the opportunity. The first step practitioners skip is separating the sources before totalling them, because each source behaves differently over time and responds to different competitive countermoves. The five that matter most in a B2B software relationship like Shaurya's are contractual costs (penalties or forfeitures written into the agreement itself), technical or compatibility costs (integrations, data formats, and workflows built around the incumbent's system), procedural or learning costs (the time employees spent becoming fluent in the incumbent's interface and rules), data costs (the historical record — filings, reconciliations, audit trails — that lives inside the incumbent's system and is painful or risky to reconstruct elsewhere), and relational costs (the trust, responsiveness, and institutional memory built up with named people on the supplier's side, which a new vendor cannot simply hand over).

Five sources of switching cost. A supplier that only manages the contractual line (penalties) is managing the source customers resent most and trust least; the durable moat lives in the technical, procedural, and data lines, which accumulate as a by-product of genuine use rather than as a threat.

The second step, and the one that separates people who merely use the term from people who understand it, is recognising that these five sources do not move in the same direction over a customer's lifetime. Contractual costs are highest at signing and decay toward zero as the term runs out — a two-year contract signed yesterday locks a customer in far more tightly, on paper, than the same contract with two months left to run. Technical, procedural, and data costs run the opposite way: they start at zero on day one, when nothing has been integrated and nobody has learned anything, and they climb steadily as the relationship matures, workflows get built, and history accumulates in the incumbent's database. A supplier who only pays attention to the contractual line — chasing renewals, writing tougher termination clauses — is managing the one source of switching cost that customers experience as a threat and resent accordingly; a supplier who lets the technical, procedural, and data lines do the work is building a moat customers barely notice because it is simply the residue of using the product well. The third step is asking, for each customer, which of the five lines is actually tall enough to matter, because a discount war fought on price alone only works if none of the five lines amounts to much — and Rohan's job that week was to find out whether that was true of Saroj Industries.

The Saroj Industries arithmetic

Rohan asked his customer-success lead to build an honest, itemised estimate of what it would actually cost Saroj Industries to move to Sumeru Books — not a defensive number designed to scare the customer, but a real one his own team could stand behind if Devinder Anand asked to see the working. Saroj had been live on Shaurya for fourteen months. In that time its six accounts staff had filed fourteen months of GST returns and e-invoices through the platform, reconciled roughly 1,800 bank transactions inside it, and connected it to Saroj's payroll system and to its bank's statement-fetch API. The team's estimate came out as follows.
