Read plainly, the base case says Devinder should not switch: even before counting the intangible relational cost, the one-time bill of ₹13.2 lakh exceeds the ₹11.9 lakh Saroj would save in year one, so the deal only turns cash-positive around month sixteen, and Devinder — a careful CFO managing working capital through a slow season — was unlikely to wear a negative first year for a payback that far out. That was the case Rohan wanted to walk into the boardroom with. But the second column shows why Sumeru's offer was cleverer than a simple discount: by paying for migration and integration itself, Sumeru does not just cut price, it directly demolishes two of the five switching-cost lines — technical and data — that would otherwise have protected Shaurya. Once those two lines are removed, the total switching cost falls to ₹6.9 lakh, comfortably below the ₹11.9 lakh in year-one savings, and the arithmetic flips to a net positive ₹5 lakh in year one alone. Sumeru was not competing on price. It was competing by buying down the customer's switching cost directly — a materially different and more dangerous move, and one that a leader who thought only in terms of "match the discount" would never have seen coming.

Eight things a learner must get right

Switching costs are not the same thing as a moat, though they can build one

A moat is a durable structural reason a competitor cannot compete away a firm's returns; switching costs are one of several mechanisms — alongside scale, network effects, brands, and the rest of Helmer's seven — that can produce that durability, but only if they are large relative to what a customer stands to gain by leaving, and only if a competitor cannot cheaply neutralise them the way Sumeru tried to. A firm can have real switching costs and still have no moat, if those costs are small next to the prize on offer or if the market has evolved standard tools — data-export utilities, migration consultants, portability regulation — that make the costs easy to pay down.

High switching costs are not the same thing as a happy customer

Devinder Anand's willingness to entertain Sumeru's call at all, after fourteen months as a Shaurya customer, was itself a warning sign that a purely contractual or technical lock-in was starting to feel less like value and more like a cage. Airlines, cable operators, and legacy ERP vendors have taught a generation of customers to associate high switching costs with resentment rather than loyalty; a product leader who reads low churn as satisfaction, without separately asking customers whether they would recommend the product, can be sitting on a renewal cliff and not know it until a well-funded rival offers to pay the toll.

The switching cost that matters is the one the customer perceives, not the one the supplier calculates

Rohan's team priced the audit-mismatch risk at ₹3 lakh using a probability model; Devinder might price the same risk at ₹50,000 if he trusts his own accountants to catch errors, or at ₹10 lakh if he has personally been through a GST scrutiny notice before. Switching-cost estimates are only useful as a guide to the customer's own mental accounting, which has to be tested through conversation, not assumed from the supplier's spreadsheet.

Switching costs decay and can be reset by events outside the supplier's control

Staff who built the fluency that created procedural lock-in eventually leave the company and take that fluency with them; a contract that once carried a heavy termination fee runs down to nothing as its term expires; a regulatory change — a new GSTN API standard, for instance — can suddenly make data that was hard to export easy to export for everyone. A supplier that built its moat in 2024 and stopped paying attention will find, in 2026, that the moat has quietly eroded.

Switching costs alone rarely survive a genuine triggering event

A steady 5 percent annual price increase a customer barely notices; a sudden 40 percent increase, a serious outage, or a change of ownership at the supplier gives the customer a reason to absorb the switching cost anyway, because the status quo itself has become the risky option. Lock-in raises the bar for a competitor to clear; it does not make the bar unclimbable, and a supplier that mistakes the first for the second tends to discover the difference at the worst possible moment.

Switching costs are often confused with network effects and multi-homing frictions, which are a related but distinct idea

A network effect makes a product more valuable as more people use it — value that is shared and forward-looking; a switching cost is a private, backward-looking cost tied to one customer's own history with one supplier. The two frequently sit side by side in marketplace businesses, and untangling them matters because the next topic this one unlocks, multi-homing, asks a related but separate question: not what it costs a customer to leave, but what stops them from simply using two suppliers at once and leaving neither.

Switching costs cannot tell you whether you deserve the customer in the first place

They measure friction, not fit. A product that is genuinely wrong for a customer's needs, propped up by high switching costs, still produces a customer who is quietly shopping, badmouthing the supplier to peers, and ready to leave the instant the friction is paid down by someone else — exactly the position Shaurya risked being in in Rohan's telling.

Before relying on a switching-cost story, a thoughtful newcomer should ask three questions

Which of the five sources is actually doing the work, and is it durable or a rented illusion built only on a contract clause? What would it cost a well-funded rival to buy down that source directly, the way Sumeru offered to absorb Saroj's migration? And is the company measuring customer sentiment separately from churn, so that lock-in is not mistaken for loyalty until the day someone tests it?

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The same five sources show up with very different weights depending on the kind of product and the age of the company, and a leader who applies a B2B mental model to a consumer product, or vice versa, will misjudge both the threat and the fix. In consumer products, switching costs are dominated by data and procedural friction that customers rarely articulate but feel strongly — years of photos in one cloud service, a decade of listening history shaping a music app's recommendations, the sheer familiarity of a banking app's layout — and relational and contractual costs are nearly absent, because individual consumers rarely have named account managers or enforceable exit penalties. In B2B software like Shaurya's, the picture inverts: contractual and technical costs are large and explicit, written into master service agreements and integration diagrams, while relational cost — the trust in a specific account manager or implementation partner — can rival the technical cost in weight, as it nearly did for Saroj. In marketplace businesses, switching cost is often smaller for either side alone than it looks, because a seller or buyer can typically list on a second marketplace at low cost, which is precisely why marketplaces lean more heavily on network effects and multi-homing frictions than on switching costs to retain participants. Company age matters just as much: an early-stage company has almost no switching costs to offer, because customers have no history built up yet, and its real defence is speed and relationship rather than lock-in; a scaled company, four or more years and hundreds of customers in like Shaurya, has switching costs accumulating as a natural by-product of tenure, but also carries the opposite risk — treating that accumulated lock-in as permanent, when in fact it has to be renewed continuously as staff turn over, contracts run down, and rivals find cheaper ways to pay it off.

Three mistakes worth watching for

The first mistake is treating low churn as proof that switching costs are working, when the real signal — the one Rohan's team had been missing until Saroj's call — is a growing gap between churn (which stays flat) and expansion revenue or referral rate (which quietly stalls). The underlying misunderstanding is conflating "customers who have not left" with "customers who would choose us again," and the cheapest diagnostic is a simple win-loss and at-risk survey run every quarter, asking existing customers, not departing ones, whether they would re-sign today at today's terms if starting fresh. The second mistake is over-investing in the contractual line — longer minimum terms, steeper exit penalties — because it is the easiest lever to pull, while under-investing in the technical, procedural, and data lines that create lock-in customers do not resent. The symptom is a churn curve with a sharp spike exactly at contract renewal dates rather than a smooth trickle, and the diagnostic is a simple cohort chart of cancellations by months-since-contract-anniversary: a spike says customers are leaving the moment the toll expires, not because the product stopped earning its place. The third mistake is assuming switching cost is uniform across the customer base and responding to a threat with an across-the-board discount, when in reality tenure, integration depth, and account size mean the true switching cost — and therefore the true risk of departure — varies enormously from customer to customer; the fix is segmenting the base by months-since-signup and integration count before deciding who actually needs a retention conversation and who does not.

What good looks like

Six months earlier, a different Shaurya customer, a Coimbatore auto-parts distributor, had received a similar approach from a rival and stayed. The difference was not a bigger discount; Shaurya's account team had, over the prior year, quietly built three things into that account without ever framing them as a retention tactic: a direct integration with the customer's e-way bill generation, a shared reconciliation dashboard the customer's own auditor had come to rely on every quarter-end, and a named implementation specialist who had personally walked the finance team through two GST notice scares. When the rival's offer arrived, the customer's own finance head ran the numbers unprompted and told Shaurya's account manager, almost as a courtesy, that the maths did not work — not because of a penalty clause, but because rebuilding what already existed would cost more than staying and take months the business did not have. That is what switching costs look like when they are earned rather than engineered: the customer defends the relationship using the supplier's own arithmetic, without being asked to.

What Rohan decided

Rohan went back to the board with the Saroj Industries ledger, not a counter-discount. He recommended against matching Sumeru's price on the contractual line, arguing that a public discount war would simply teach every customer to call and threaten, and instead proposed two changes: first, that Shaurya offer to co-fund migration and integration costs, but only for customers past a minimum tenure where genuine embedded value already existed — turning the switching-cost ledger into an honest negotiating table rather than a penalty; and second, that the company build, for every new customer from day one, the kind of integration and reconciliation depth the Coimbatore account had accumulated by accident, so that lock-in was designed in as a by-product of good onboarding rather than left to chance fourteen months later. Devinder Anand stayed, in the end, on a renegotiated eighteen-month term at a modest discount, persuaded less by the number than by Shaurya's account manager sitting across the table from him one more time. Two questions worth sitting with follow directly from this decision: whether your own product's switching costs would survive a rival who, instead of cutting price, offered to pay them off directly — and which of the five sources of switching cost your business is currently building on purpose, versus which have simply piled up as an accident of time. The next idea worth studying from here is multi-homing: what happens, and what a supplier should do, when a customer's answer to high switching costs is not to leave at all, but simply to start using a second supplier alongside the first.
